name: Charitable hospital care at Caesarea in Cappadocia
summary: Basil of Caesarea founded a charitable complex where the sick poor, lepers and travellers were lodged and treated by physicians, in operation by about 372 CE.
description: Near Caesarea in Cappadocia, Basil built a complex of church and dwellings that lodged strangers, the sick and lepers free of charge and gave them professional physicians, paid for by donations from the rich. His letters show medical staff there by 372 and a largely complete complex by 373. Similar Christian hospitals followed elsewhere in the Roman Empire; whether Basil's was a general hospital or chiefly a leprosarium is debated.

impact.note: The source says similar Christian hospitals spread through the Roman Empire and were commonplace within a century (most of one civilisation, for generations); free inpatient care by physicians was a new capability; and a continuing line of hospital institutions followed.

why: Heyne ties the foundation to Christian teaching on sharing wealth with the poor and to the impetus of a famine in Cappadocia.

date.label: by 372 CE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: By 372 the complex had professional medical personnel, and by 373 it was complete enough for Basil to invite fellow bishops to visit.

evidence.supports: By 372 it had professional medical personnel; and by 373 it was sufficiently complete

date.label: c. 372 CE

events.statement: One of Basil's letters that refer to the complex was written around 372 to the local governor.

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Read Caner, Not a Hospital but a Leprosarium: Basil's Basilias (Dumbarton Oaks Papers 72, 2018), and settle whether the complex was a hospital or a leprosarium.
Check the earlier Christian hostels and poorhouses of the 340s and 350s, and the Mihintale and Indian claims with their dated evidence, any of which could displace 'first known'.
The lead's Constantinople foundations and the continuity into Byzantine, Islamic and Latin hospitals need their own sources (Miller, The Birth of the Hospital in the Byzantine Empire).
The only source is an essay in a medical-humanities journal; a historian's monograph should replace it.

research.note: Heyne argues it was likely the first true hospital because, unlike Roman valetudinaria and Asclepian temples, it combined inpatient lodging, professional physicians and free care; the claim is contested (Caner 2018) and South Asian claims were not checked.
